## The idea

Move a note head one staff position upward and its letter advances by one. The
corresponding sounding pitch may rise by one semitone or by two. Printed notation
therefore uses a diatonic coordinate system of letter steps, while MIDI numbers
use a chromatic coordinate system in which every increment is a semitone. A
decoder must translate between them rather than treating one visual step as one
MIDI step.

The *staff* consists of five lines and the four spaces between them. A *treble
clef* fixes G4 on the second line from the bottom; all nearby letters follow from
that anchor in the repeating A-to-G cycle. Middle C sits on its own short ledger
line below the staff. If middle C is coordinate zero, the bottom treble line E4
is coordinate two, with the intervening D4 in the space below.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 90
use_synth :piano

letters = [:c, :d, :e, :f, :g, :a, :b]
semitones = {c: 0, d: 2, e: 4, f: 5, g: 7, a: 9, b: 11}

define :staff_record do |position, letters, semitones|
  letter = letters[position % 7]
  octave = 4 + (position / 7).floor
  midi = 12 * (octave + 1) + semitones[letter]
  {position: position, letter: letter, octave: octave, midi: midi}
end

# Eight printed positions: bottom line through the space above the staff.
printed_positions = [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]

printed_positions.each do |position|
  record = staff_record(position, letters, semitones)
  puts "position #{position}: #{record[:letter]}#{record[:octave]} midi=#{record[:midi]}"
  play record[:midi], release: 0.55
  sleep 0.75
end

# One-octave cheat sheet from middle C to the next C.
(0..7).each { |position| puts staff_record(position, letters, semitones) }
```

The eight positions rise in consecutive letters from E4 through E5. On the page,
each move is exactly one line-or-space step. In the log, the MIDI differences
alternate irregularly between one and two semitones, because E-F and B-C are
smaller than the other natural-letter steps. This is the translation the
coordinate function is responsible for making.

## Change one thing

1. Replace the list with `[0, 2, 4, 6]`. Starting at middle C and skipping every
   other diatonic position selects C4, E4, G4, and B4. Play them together and
   the regular visual skips become a C-major seventh chord.
2. Alternate positions `2` and `3`: E to F is one staff step and one semitone.
   Then alternate `3` and `4`: F to G occupies the same visual distance but spans
   two semitones. Keep the tempo fixed so pitch distance carries the contrast.
3. Add positions `-1` and `-2`. Ruby's modulo and floor division extend the
   letter and octave cycles below middle C without requiring a second lookup
   table for negative coordinates.

## Why it works

The seven letter names form a ring. Position modulo seven selects the letter;
floor division counts completed letter cycles and adjusts the octave. Only after
those diatonic coordinates are known does the `semitones` hash convert the name
to a chromatic distance. The two spaces remain separate in the code because they
measure different things.

Treble clef is an offset convention: by assigning a known pitch to one line, it
determines every other position. Memorised line and space mnemonics can provide
quick checks, but they split one continuous system into two lists. The coordinate
model handles lines, spaces, and ledger lines with the same operation, which is
more useful when a melody leaves the five-line staff.

Accidentals and key signatures modify the chromatic result in Lesson 40 without
moving the note head. F and F-sharp occupy the same staff coordinate because
both retain the letter F; the sharp changes the final semitone lookup. This is
another reason not to infer MIDI distance directly from vertical spacing.

Printed notation carries time as well as pitch through note heads, stems, beams,
rests, and dots. Those marks are deliberately absent from the decoder here so
vertical position is the only changing field. Lesson 41 restores rhythm by
placing pitch coordinate and duration in separate event keys. A beam can then
change timing without becoming entangled in pitch translation.

## Take it further

Generate a Markdown table for positions `-2` through `10`. Include coordinate,
line-or-space classification, letter, octave, Sonic Pi symbol, and MIDI integer,
and mark middle C plus the five treble lines. Then choose eight note heads from
a printed source, enter their coordinates, and play the decoded sequence without
copying note names from an existing transcription. Use the source page to check
the coordinates and the log to check the conversion; they catch different errors.
